claims.text: Greg Short (founder of Bloom, a greens supplement brand) asserts that immediately reinvesting all revenue back into inventory rather than consuming it on lifestyle purchases (e.g., a Rolex or sports car) is the decision that accelerated Bloom's competitive lead over rivals. The mechanism is compounding reinvestment velocity: each dollar cycled back into production before competitors can react widens the supply and market-presence gap, not over months but over days.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: following a high-volume sales event where cash is immediately available
competitor behavior does not match reinvestment speed
claims.mechanism: Reinvesting 100% of proceeds into the next purchase order before competitors act compounds supply availability and brand momentum; the opportunity cost of consumption is the compounding advantage foregone.
bounded_by: Applies when working capital can be deployed immediately into replicable inventory; may not apply to bespoke or made-to-order products with long lead times

examples.text: On one day, Bloom generated $1.36 million in sales within 12 hours. The following day, when that money hit the bank account, Greg Short called the manufacturer and placed a $1.36 million purchase order for more greens inventory, doubling down the entire day's revenue rather than spending any of it on personal rewards. Short credits this pattern of immediate full reinvestment as the primary reason Bloom outpaced competitors faster than expected.

practices.text: After a major sales event, do not take your foot off the gas: place the next inventory purchase order with the full proceeds before lifestyle temptation can redirect capital.
